problem: The direction of the wavelength–frequency relation is inverted. Since f = c/λ, a smaller wavelength gap Δλ gives a smaller frequency gap: Δf ≈ (c/λ²)·Δλ. Closer wavelengths therefore mean narrower bands in Hz, not wider ones. A student who memorises 'closer wavelengths = wider bands in Hz' will get the conversion backwards.
fix: Treating WDM as a new mechanism. It is FDM at optical frequencies, and wavelength and frequency are inversely related through f = c/λ, so a wavelength gap Δλ corresponds to a frequency gap Δf ≈ (c/λ²)·Δλ. Closer wavelengths (smaller Δλ) mean narrower bands in Hz, and the same Δλ gives a larger Δf at shorter wavelengths.

problem: The sentence 'Statistical TDM divides time but not fairly, which is why it needs addresses' gives a wrong cause. Addresses are needed because slot position no longer identifies the user when slots are handed out on demand, not because the sharing is unfair.
fix: Statistical TDM divides time on demand, so a slot's position no longer tells the receiver whose data it carries; that is why every slot must carry an address.

problem: The text says 12 channels of 4 kHz fill a 48 kHz group with no guard bands, while the formula above says bandwidth = ΣBi + (n − 1)·Bguard. A student can read this as a contradiction.
fix: Add one clause: the 4 kHz figure is the channel spacing and already includes the guard band between neighbouring voice channels, so 12 × 4 kHz = 48 kHz needs no extra gap.
